answer:
Full analysis executed (script saved at `analysis.py`, run in workspace). Results:

**(1) LMC regressions** (GNIpc = constant 2015 US$; edu = adjusted savings: education expenditure, % of GNI; OLS, homoskedastic SEs, linear time trend)

Level model — ln(GNIpc_t) ~ edu_{t−k} + trend:
| k | n | β_edu | SE | t | p | β_trend | R² |
|---|---|-------|------|------|--------|---------|------|
| 0 | 41 | **−0.200** | 0.049 | −4.07 | <0.001 | 0.01928 | 0.919 |
| 1 | 40 | **−0.212** | 0.047 | −4.47 | <0.001 | 0.02005 | 0.929 |
| 5 | 36 | **−0.099** | 0.044 | −2.27 | 0.023 | 0.02425 | 0.951 |

Growth model — Δln(GNIpc_t) ~ Δ(du_{t−k}) + trend:
| k | n | β_edu | SE | t | p | β_trend | R² |
|---|---|-------|------|------|--------|---------|------|
| 0 | 40 | **+0.040** | 0.015 | 2.61 | 0.009 | 0.00128 | 0.380 |
| 1 | 39 | +0.008 | 0.015 | 0.52 | 0.601 | 0.00137 | 0.401 |
| 5 | 35 | −0.005 | 0.013 | −0.38 | 0.707 | 0.00085 | 0.246 |

Read: the only robust LMC association is **contemporaneous** — a 1pp higher edu share in year t is associated with ~4pp higher GDP growth that same year; with 1- and 5-year lags the effect vanishes. The negative level coefficients are time-series confounding (the share fell 2008–2015 exactly while GNI grew fastest), not evidence education hurts income.

**(2) SSA 5-point descriptive, 2011–2015 (non-inferential):**
- Edu share (% of GNI): mean 3.414, range 3.154–3.651 (0.497); declining, 3.651 → 3.154
- GNIpc (2015 US$): mean 1589.0, range 1555.3–1634.3 (79.0); rising, 1555.3 → 1634.3
- Direction: **opposite** — edu share down while income up
- Pearson r (levels, n=5) = **−0.966**; r (YoY changes, n=4) = −0.456 — descriptive only, no inference (5 points; 2011 is the first SSA GNIpc year in the file)

**(3) Structured comparison:** LMC (41 years) shows a small, contemporaneous, non-lagged association between education-expenditure-share changes and GDP growth (β=0.040, t=2.61), while its level association is negative once the common trend is controlled — i.e., the two series are largely trend-driven and weakly coupled year-to-year. SSA (5 years) shows the opposite co-movement: a declining expenditure share alongside steady income growth (r=−0.97, n=5). Neither group exhibits evidence of a strong positive association, and with only two aggregate rows per year and a 5-year SSA outcome window, a differential "effect" between groups is not estimable from this data.

**(4) Draft hypothesis (for the submission answer):**

> Using World Bank group-level data (1975–2015), education expenditure is measured as adjusted savings for education as a share of GNI (NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS) and income as GNI per capita in constant 2015 US$ (NY.GNP.PCAP.KD). For lower-middle-income (developing) countries, the association between changes in the education-expenditure share and per-capita GDP growth is small and contemporaneous — a 1 percentage-point higher share in a given year is associated with roughly 4 percentage points higher growth in that same year (β = 0.040, t = 2.6, n = 40) and becomes insignificant at 1- and 5-year lags, while the level association is actually negative (β ≈ −0.2) once the common time trend is controlled. For Sub-Saharan Africa, per-capita income is observed only for 2011–2015, a window in which the education-expenditure share fell from 3.65% to 3.15% of GNI while GNI per capita rose from US$1,555 to US$1,634 — a negative co-movement (r = −0.97, n = 5, descriptive only). The data therefore do not support the hypothesis that education expenditure is associated with per-capita GDP more strongly in Sub-Saharan Africa than among developing (lower-middle-income) countries; if anything, the data suggest the association is weak in both groups and cannot be reliably estimated for Sub-Saharan Africa from this five-year window.

(4 sentences; names both groups, the exact variable, states the groups do not show a differential stronger effect in SSA; non-causal language throughout.)
